postTitle: Shared Households: Money for Three or More Adults
topic: An equal split of shared bills is equal in euros and very unequal in weight

assumptions.notes: Four adults share a flat. Net monthly incomes: Alma €5,000, Ben €3,000, Chidi €2,000, Dana €1,000; total €11,000. Shared costs €3,200 a month: €2,400 rent, €300 utilities, €500 food. Equal split: €800 each, which is 16%, 27%, 40% and 80% of each income; 80 ÷ 16 = 5, a five to one gap. Income split: €3,200 ÷ €11,000 = 29.1%; Alma €1,455, Ben €873, Chidi €582, Dana €291. Illustrative.

hookVariants.narration: Four flatmates split the bills equally. For one, that is sixteen percent of her pay. For another, eighty.
Splitting the rent equally with flatmates feels fair. The numbers can say something very different.
Same flat, same share of the bills, and one flatmate carries five times the weight.

beats.narration: Four adults share a flat. Rent, utilities and food come to three thousand two hundred euros a month.
Split equally, everyone pays eight hundred. Alma earns five thousand, so for her that is sixteen percent.
Dana earns one thousand. The same eight hundred is eighty percent of her income.
beats.subtext: The same €800, a very different weight

beats.narration: Equal in euros. Five to one in how heavy the bill feels.
beats.subtext: In how heavy the bill feels

beats.narration: Split by income instead, and everyone pays twenty nine percent of their own pay. Level weight, but everyone shares what they earn.
So before agreeing a split, many households work out each share as a percentage of each income, for every method on the table.

caption.instagram:
Four flatmates split the bills equally. For one, that is 16% of her pay. For another, 80%.

Four adults share a flat, with net incomes from €1,000 to €5,000 and €3,200 of shared costs a month. An equal split is €800 each: 16% of Alma's income, 80% of Dana's, a five to one gap in how heavy the same bill feels. A split by income has everyone pay 29% of their own, and asks each person to share what they earn. Room based, hybrid and capped splits sit in between. None of them is the right answer.

The split check: for each method on the table, each share divided by each net income.
